phases.title: All Souls

entries.title: Soul cakes
entries.account: On the first of November Ambrose Trencher baked forty soul cakes for All Souls, as the old Academy did, and moved the sack of onions off the little west door.

castMemories.memory: Ambrose baked forty soul cakes for All Souls and moved the onions off the west door without knowing why.
castMemories.aside: Forty soul cakes. And I moved the onions. Don't ask me why. My hands knew before I did.

entries.title: The knock
entries.account: That night the Guest knocked three times at the west door, saying the old souling rhyme. Ambrose Trencher gave them a soul cake and a seat by the fire, and didn't ask their name.

castMemories.memory: Ambrose fed a stranger at the west door on All Souls' Eve and didn't ask their name.
castMemories.aside: Fed them first. You always feed them first. The questions keep.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says somebody came in at the west door on All Souls and Ambrose let them sit by the fire.

castMemories.memory: The Guest knocked at the west door. Ambrose gave it a soul cake and a place by the fire before asking its name.
castMemories.aside: He moved the onions. There was a place by the fire.

entries.title: The pots
entries.account: In the morning every pot in the Kitchens had been scrubbed and hung biggest to smallest. Ambrose Trencher left them that way.

castMemories.memory: In the morning every pot in the Kitchens had been scrubbed and hung biggest to smallest.
castMemories.aside: Somebody hung my pots wrong. Beautifully wrong. I haven't moved them.

entries.title: Three nights
entries.account: On the third evening Dr. Vellum asked to examine the stranger, now called the Guest. Ambrose refused. Professor Lydia Boggle confirmed the oldest house rule: three nights at the hearth make a guest, and nobody may harm a guest or turn one out.

castMemories.memory: Dr. Vellum asked to examine the Guest and Ambrose said no: three nights at the hearth makes a guest.
castMemories.aside: Three nights of porridge and not one measurement. I've written that down instead.

castMemories.memory: Professor Boggle told the Kitchens the oldest house rule: three nights at the hearth, and nobody may turn a guest out.
castMemories.aside: I keep the rooms. I know the rules the rooms keep. I'd rather I didn't, this month.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says the Guest can't be turned out now. Three nights at the hearth. Professor Boggle looked it up.

entries.title: The T in treacle
entries.account: On Bonfire Night Penny Blackletter found the first letter missing from The Middlemost Cookery, Ambrose's estate-sale cookbook: the T in treacle, on the page for parkin. It had been there on Sunday.

castMemories.memory: Penny found the first letter missing from The Middlemost Cookery: the T in treacle, gone between Sunday and Bonfire Night.
castMemories.aside: The T's gone from treacle. I've checked my eyes. My eyes are fine.

entries.title: Never the other thing
entries.account: At the bonfire Professor Kyle Momort told students never to thank the Guest. To say I'm grateful, if they must say something, and never the other thing.

castMemories.memory: At the bonfire Professor Momort warned students never to thank the Guest, only to say they were grateful.
castMemories.aside: Never the other thing. I've said so. I'll say it again at breakfast.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says you're not allowed to thank the Guest. Momort said so, plainly, which he never does.

entries.title: Martinmas
entries.account: At the Martinmas supper the food in the Great Hall tasted of nothing. Serenity Brown laughed, and told the Hall she hadn't tasted anything since October. Ambrose Trencher halved the loaves for Martinmas and gave the extra half to the Guest.

castMemories.memory: At the Martinmas supper Serenity told the whole Hall she hasn't tasted anything since the Count.
castMemories.aside: Everybody knows now. It's oddly nice. Six weeks of paper and now we're all eating it.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says Serenity can't taste anything. Hasn't since October. She laughed and told everyone.

castMemories.memory: On Martinmas Ambrose halved the loaves, as Saint Martin halved his cloak, and gave the Guest an extra half.
castMemories.aside: Halved the bread. Gave it the extra half. You don't skip a guest because the soup's gone wrong.

entries.title: Two hundred and fourteen
entries.account: Penny Blackletter counted two hundred and fourteen letters missing from The Middlemost Cookery and found that only the recipes somebody was still making had kept theirs. Ambrose Trencher said, "Then we cook."

castMemories.memory: Penny counted two hundred and fourteen missing letters and found only the recipes being made stayed whole.
castMemories.aside: Two hundred and fourteen. And a pattern. I'd rather have the pattern than the sleep.

castMemories.memory: When Penny showed Ambrose that only the recipes being made stayed whole, he tied his apron tighter and said they'd cook.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says everybody's cooking now. Even the second-years. Especially the second-years. Stand back.

entries.title: The Kitchens full
entries.account: That afternoon the Kitchens filled. Wicker Eddies made his first omelette. Soren Ng laid out nine teaspoons of tastes on the dresser. Min-seo Kim asked the Guest what it needed, and it said, "Something I used to have."

castMemories.memory: Wicker made his first omelette and carried it the whole length of the long table to Serenity.
castMemories.aside: Brown on one side. Runny on the other. She ate all of it. She can't even taste it.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says Wicker cooked. Actually cooked. An omelette. With eggshell in it.

castMemories.memory: Soren laid out nine teaspoons of tastes on the dresser for Serenity, with numbered slips.
castMemories.aside: Nine spoons. She kept the first slip. That's all I know so far. That's plenty.

castMemories.memory: Min-seo was the only one who asked the Guest what it needed, and it said something it used to have.
castMemories.aside: Nobody'd asked it anything in two weeks. Two weeks! I'd have bitten someone.

entries.title: Three in the morning
entries.account: In the small hours the Guest made Serenity Brown an offer: the taste of things, for one evening's memory. What she answered is hers to tell.

castMemories.memory: At three in the morning the Guest offered Serenity the taste of things back, for one evening's memory.

entries.title: Stir-up Sunday
entries.account: On Stir-up Sunday the whole Academy stirred the pudding and wished. The Guest stirred too, and said its wish out loud: home. The Headmistress stood in the doorway and didn't come in.

castMemories.memory: On Stir-up Sunday the Headmistress stood in the Kitchens' doorway, watched the Guest stir, and went back upstairs.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says the Headmistress came down on Stir-up Sunday, stood in the door, and went away again.

entries.title: Under the endpaper
entries.account: That night the page under the endpaper of The Middlemost Cookery came clear for the first time in thirty years. It was titled A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots. Ambrose Trencher read it three times.

castMemories.memory: On Stir-up Sunday the page under the endpaper came back: A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.
castMemories.aside: Thirty years. It was at the back the whole time. Waiting for somebody to cook enough.

entries.title: A place at the table
entries.account: Supper was at the long table in the Kitchens. Ambrose Trencher set one place for whoever was missing, and nobody sat in it. Penny Blackletter said she'd set it for her grandmother.

castMemories.memory: At the long table Penny said she'd set the empty chair for her grandmother, who taught her to check twice.
Ambrose set a place at the long table for whoever's missing, and nobody sat in it.
castMemories.gossip: {teller} says Ambrose set a place at the long table for nobody, and nobody asked why. Everybody knew.

entries.title: The bowl
entries.account: On the last day of November Ambrose Trencher cooked the bowl from the page: oats in milk, salt, honey, butter, cold cream round the edge. He set it on the hearth and didn't say who it was for.

castMemories.memory: On the last day of November Ambrose cooked the bowl from the page and set it on the hearth without saying who it was for.
castMemories.aside: Oats. Thirty years and it was oats. I'd have laughed if I wasn't busy.

entries.title: Unattributed
entries.account: By the end of the last night there was a white bowl on the west step, very fine, with a single black thorn laid beside it. Penny Blackletter filed it under Unattributed.

castMemories.memory: Penny filed a white bowl and a black thorn found on the west step under Unattributed.
castMemories.aside: Unattributed. I've never used that drawer before. I don't like how easily it opened.

catchUp.title: Everybody Still Has to Eat
catchUp.body:
October was the month a Count got out of his book. He's back in it now. Serenity Brown came out of it hearing pages turn in the walls, and she's got a word for that: Nightbound. The East Stacks are open again. The Academy's tired.

So November starts in the Kitchens, where it's warm. It's All Souls. Ambrose Trencher has baked forty soul cakes, the way the old Academy did, with a cross cut in every one. And he's moved the sack of onions off the little west door. Nobody uses that door. Nobody's used it in a hundred years.

I've asked him why he moved them. He says his hands knew before he did.
catchUp.openQuestion: Who's going to come to the west door?

catchUp.title: The Guest
catchUp.body:
On All Souls' Eve somebody knocked at the Kitchens' west door, three times, saying the old souling rhyme. Ambrose gave them a soul cake and a seat by the fire, and didn't ask their name. They're small. They wear a green coat that's far too big for them. They've been here ever since.

The students call them the Guest. Every morning every pot in the Kitchens is scrubbed, and nobody did it. The Guest eats everything it's given and never says thank you. Dr. Vellum wanted to examine it. Professor Boggle says the oldest house rule won't allow it: three nights at the hearth, and nobody can turn a guest out.

I can't smell it. Everybody smells of something.

catchUp.title: The T in Treacle
catchUp.body:
A stranger the students call the Guest came to the Kitchens on All Souls, and Ambrose let it stay. It eats everything and never says thank you, and by the oldest house rule nobody can turn it out.

On Bonfire Night Penny found a letter missing from Ambrose's old cookbook, The Middlemost Cookery. The T had gone from treacle, on the page for parkin. It was there on Sunday. Penny checks the book every morning now.

At the bonfire, Professor Momort told everybody never to thank the Guest. Say I'm grateful, he said, if you have to say something. Never the other thing.

catchUp.title: Martinmas Goes Flat
catchUp.body:
Since All Souls a stranger called the Guest has been living in the Kitchens. Nobody can turn it out, and nobody's allowed to thank it. Letters keep vanishing from Ambrose's cookbook.

Then, at the Martinmas supper, nobody could taste their food. Goose, potatoes, gravy: all of it tasted of nothing. Serenity Brown laughed out loud, and told the whole Hall she hasn't tasted anything since October. "Now you know," she said.

Ambrose halved the loaves for Martinmas, the way Saint Martin halved his cloak for a beggar. He gave the Guest the extra half.
catchUp.openQuestion: Can anybody get the taste back?

catchUp.title: Then We Cook
catchUp.body:
A stranger called the Guest has lived in the Kitchens since All Souls. Since it came, the Academy's food has gone flat, and letters keep going missing from Ambrose's cookbook.

Penny counted them: two hundred and fourteen. Then she found the pattern. The only recipes keeping their letters are the ones somebody's still making. A recipe only stays alive while somebody's cooking it.

So Ambrose said, "Then we cook." And now everybody does. Wicker made his first omelette. Soren laid out nine teaspoons of tastes. Min-seo asked the Guest what it needed. It said something it used to have.

Ambrose says your kitchen counts too.

catchUp.title: A Wish Said Out Loud
catchUp.body:
The Guest came to the Kitchens on All Souls. Since then the food's gone flat and letters have vanished from Ambrose's cookbook, and the whole Academy's been cooking to keep the recipes alive.

One night at three in the morning, the Guest made Serenity an offer: the taste of things, for one evening's memory. What she answered is hers to tell.

On Stir-up Sunday everybody stirred the pudding and wished. The Guest stirred too, and said its wish out loud. You must never do that. It said: home. The Headmistress watched from the doorway and didn't come in.

That night a page came back in Ambrose's cookbook, from under the endpaper, after thirty years.

catchUp.title: A Place for Whoever's Missing
catchUp.body:
A stranger called the Guest came to the Kitchens on All Souls and has stayed all month. The Academy's been cooking to keep its recipes alive. On Stir-up Sunday the Guest said its wish out loud: home.

The page Ambrose has looked for for thirty years came back that night. It's called A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.

Supper's been at the long table in the Kitchens. Ambrose set one place for whoever's missing, and nobody sat in it, and nobody asked. The Guest ate with everybody else, the ordinary way. It looked like it belonged somewhere.

catchUp.title: The Bowl Set Down
catchUp.body:
On All Souls a stranger came souling to the Kitchens' west door, and Ambrose Trencher fed it. The Academy called it the Guest. While it stayed, the food went flat and Ambrose's old cookbook lost its letters, until everybody started cooking to keep the recipes alive.

On the last day of November Ambrose cooked the page he'd waited thirty years for. It was oats, in milk, with honey and butter and cold cream round the edge. He set the bowl on the hearth and didn't say who it was for. Everybody knew.

In the morning there was a white bowl on the west step, and a black thorn beside it.

beats.title: A Potato
beats.body:
Professor Boggle puts a potato on the front desk of the Glint Hall and sits down and looks at it.

That's how the lesson starts. Nobody says anything for nearly a minute. It's a very ordinary potato. It's got a bit of mud on it still, and two eyes on one side, and a dent where somebody dropped it.

“Ambrose told me something thirty years ago,” she says, at last. “He said a potato's owed the same attention as saffron. I thought he was being funny. He wasn't. He's never been funny in his life.”

She hands out potatoes. One each. Then she hands out peelers, and a sheet of paper, and a pencil.

“Write down five true things about your potato before you peel it,” she says. “Then five more after. Nothing clever. Nothing about what it means. What it is.”

The Glint Hall goes quiet in the way it only goes quiet when everybody's looking at something properly. Somebody finds out their potato smells like a cellar. Somebody finds a tiny green sprout curled up in one of the eyes like a fist. Somebody peels theirs and says, out loud, very surprised, “It's *wet* inside,” and nobody laughs, because it's true, and they'd never noticed.

At the end Professor Boggle collects the potatoes in a basket. She's taking them to the Kitchens.

“Nothing's wasted,” she says. “That's the other half of the lesson. The magic in a kitchen isn't the glamorous sort. It's paying attention to something cheap until it gives up being ordinary, and then feeding somebody with it.”

You've got mud on your thumb from the potato. I can smell it through my cover. It smells like the start of soup.
beats.report: Professor Boggle taught the Glint Hall to write five true things about a potato before and after peeling it.

beats.title: A Meal Is Fuel
beats.body:
Dr. Vellum weighs a bowl of porridge on a brass scale and writes the number on the board.

“Four hundred and ten grams,” Vellum says. “Oats, milk, salt. This is fuel. It goes in. You go on. That's the whole arrangement, and it's a good one, and I'm going to show you how to notice it working.”

The Still Room's warm and quiet. Everybody gets a bowl and a card. On one side of the card it says BEFORE and on the other it says AFTER. Before you eat, you write down how your hands feel and how loud the room is and whether you can think in straight lines. After you eat, you write it all down again.

It's a good lesson. I like it more than I meant to. Your hands are cold before. They're warmer after. You write that down, and it turns out to be true, and that's a strange thing to find out about porridge.

“Who's right?” says somebody at the back.

beats.title: Don't Hurry the Onions
beats.body:
Ambrose doesn't teach classes. He's said so, many times. He feeds people, and that's a different job.

Today he's teaching a class.

There are twelve students at the long table in the Kitchens, each with a chopping board, a knife and one onion. Ambrose stands at the end in his apron with his arms folded.

“Chop it,” he says. “Small. Doesn't have to be pretty.”

They chop. Eyes stream. Somebody says a word Penny would write down. The Kitchens fill up with that sharp, wet, green smell that makes you want to blink.

Then he puts a big flat pan on the range, and a lump of butter in it, and waits.

“Listen,” he says.

The butter goes from quiet to a small busy hiss, like rain on a tent. When it's foaming, he tips all twelve onions in at once, and the whole pan *roars*, and then settles into a low wet crackle.

“That's the sound,” says Ambrose. “Remember it. Now don't touch it.”

“For how long?”

“Longer than you want to.”

It takes twenty minutes. Nobody's allowed to turn the heat up. The onions go from white to clear to gold to the brown of a good violin, and the smell changes every five minutes, sharp to sweet to something so warm you could sleep in it.

“That's all I know,” Ambrose says, at the end. “Every good thing starts like this. The trick isn't the onions. The trick's not hurrying. Everybody hurries.”

He gives everyone a spoonful. It tastes of something. I'm almost sure it does.

I write down the sound. I've never kept a sound before.
beats.report: Ambrose taught twelve students to soften onions in butter without hurrying, and to listen to the pan.

beats.title: A Note from the Kitchens
beats.body:
Reader—

I don't write letters. Penny says I have to write one, because the Book keeps asking her what I'm like, and she says she's tired of explaining.

So.

It's a strange month down here. You'll have heard. There's a guest by my fire and the soup's gone thin and my old cookbook's losing its letters, and I don't know what any of that means, and I'm not going to pretend I do.

What I do know is this. Everybody has to eat. That doesn't stop because a month's gone strange.

So this week, feed somebody. That's all. It doesn't have to be anything. Toast counts. A cup of tea put down by somebody's elbow counts. Make it, put it in front of them, and walk off before they can make a fuss.

And don't write back to say thanks. I won't read that part.

—A. Trencher

*P.S. If you've got a thing you make that isn't written down anywhere, write it down. I mean it. They don't keep otherwise.*
beats.report: Ambrose wrote to the Reader: feed somebody this week, and write down the thing you make that isn't written anywhere.

beats.title: Never the Other Thing
beats.body:
Reader—

A short note, because you'll hear it said wrong at breakfast.

The rule is: you don't thank it. Not ever. Not for the pots, not for the trays, not if it passes you the salt. Say you're grateful, if something has to be said. Say nothing, if you can manage that. Never the other thing.

It isn't rudeness. Thanks are a kind of wage, and a paid thing's free to go, and some things, once they go, go a very long way and come back different. There's a door at the west end of the Kitchens with a sack of onions against it. I've never asked who put them there. I've a fair idea why.

Now the part nobody else will tell you. I like this month.

There's a stranger at the hearth, and a law nobody remembers making, and a cookbook going quiet one letter at a time. Something's at stake down there. Most months the Academy eats its supper and nothing's at stake at all, and it's very pleasant, and in a year nobody remembers a single mouthful.

Remember this one. Mind your manners and know where the doors are. Then go and sit nearer the fire than you strictly need to.

—K. Momort

*P.S. If it ever offers you anything, ask what it costs before you ask what it is.*
beats.report: Professor Momort wrote to the Reader: never thank the Guest, say you're grateful, and if it offers anything, ask the cost first.

beats.title: Paper
beats.body:
Hello—

I'm writing this on the end of the long table at two in the morning. That's where I am at two in the morning now. Ambrose leaves soup on the warm corner of the range. I eat it. It tastes like paper.

Everybody knows that now. I told the whole Great Hall at Martinmas. I didn't mean to. It came out of me sideways, like a sneeze.

I want to tell you something I haven't told anyone, because you were there in October, carrying the Book, and you've seen worse than me eating soup at two in the morning.

The worst bit isn't the food. It's the rain. I used to stand on the roof and stick my tongue out at it. It tasted of tin and sky. That's gone too. I keep going up there anyway. I stand in it with my mouth open like an idiot and wait.

Nothing yet.

The Guest watches me eat. It leans over everybody's plate before they do. When it gets to mine, it stops, and looks at me, and moves on. As if there's nothing there.

I think there isn't. That's the funny part.

Don't worry about me. I'm only telling you because it's two in the morning and the soup's gone cold.

—S.

*P.S. Go and taste something for me. Something sharp. Tell the Book what it was.*
beats.report: Serenity wrote at two in the morning: since October everything tastes of paper, even the rain.

beats.title: Kitchen Law
beats.body:
Professor Boggle found this in a drawer at the back of the Pantry, under a stack of old tea towels and a mousetrap with nothing in it. The ink's gone the brown of strong tea. The handwriting's older than anybody in the building. She's pinned it inside the Pantry door, and Penny's copied it out for me, word for word.

*THE RULES OF THIS KITCHEN*

*Feed the one at the door before you ask who they are.*

*Three nights at the hearth make a guest. A guest is not to be harmed nor turned out, until they go of their own choosing.*

*Never thank the ones who keep this house. Thanks are a wage, and a paid thing has to go.*

*Set the bowl down at night. Say nothing about who it is for.*

*Scrub your own pots. If they are scrubbed in the morning and you did not do it, say nothing, and leave the bowl.*

At the bottom somebody's added a line in pencil, much later, in a different hand:

*We stopped setting the bowl. I don't know who decided.*

Penny's put a small question mark beside that line. I've put my corner on it, very lightly. I don't like it.
beats.report: Professor Boggle found the Kitchens' old rules in the Pantry: feed the guest first, never thank the ones who keep the house, set the bowl down at night.

storyScenes.title: The Knock
storyScenes.opening:
The soul cakes are cooling on the long table.

There are forty of them, flat and round and the colour of a good brown paper bag, and every one has a cross cut into the top before it went in the oven. Ambrose Trencher's the Academy's cook, and the Kitchens are his. He makes them every All Souls. Nobody asked him to. The old Academy did it, so he does it. He says a custom's like a pot: if nobody uses it, it rusts.

The Kitchens are warm and nearly dark. The big fire's been banked down to a red heap. The pots hang in their rows over the range, and the long pine table runs away into the shadows like a road. It smells of nutmeg and hot currants and the end of a long day.

You've set me on the end of the table, by the cakes. I can smell them through my cover. Paper remembers every kitchen, and I'm remembering this one as hard as I can.

Then somebody knocks.

It isn't the door from the Great Hall. Everybody uses that one. It isn't the yard door where the milk comes in. It's the little door at the west end, past the Pantry. It's low and black, with iron studs, and its bolts are painted over so thick they look like knuckles. Nobody uses the west door. Ambrose keeps a sack of onions against it. Except he moved the onions this morning, and couldn't say why.

The knock comes three times. It's polite. It's patient. It sounds like somebody who's knocked on a great many doors.

Ambrose wipes his hands on his apron. He looks at the west door for a long moment. He looks at the soul cakes. Then he goes to it.

The door sticks. He has to put his shoulder to it. It opens with a sound like a stair giving way, and the cold comes in all at once, a wet black November cold that smells of leaves and stone.

Somebody's standing on the step.

They're small. They come up to about Ambrose's elbow. They're wearing a coat that's far too big for them, a long green coat with brass buttons, the kind a grand person might've worn to church a very long time ago. It's gone ragged at the hem. It's dark with rain. The hood's up, and I can't see a face under it. I can see two hands, folded in front, and they're very clean.

The somebody says, in a voice like a spoon in an empty bowl:

“A soul, a soul, a soul cake. Please, good master, a soul cake. An apple, a pear, a plum or a cherry, any good thing to make us all merry.”

It's the old souling rhyme. Children used to go door to door with it on All Souls, a long time ago, asking for cakes and saying a prayer for the house's dead in return. I know it from three different books. I've never heard anybody say it out loud before. It sounds older out loud.

Ambrose doesn't ask who they are. That's the first thing I notice, and I notice it very hard.

He takes a soul cake off the tray. He puts it in their clean hands. Then he steps back from the door, so the way's clear.

“Come and sit by the fire,” he says. “You've had a long walk.”

The somebody comes in.

They walk the way a cat walks into a new house: along the wall, and slowly, touching nothing. They sit on the low stool by the banked fire. They eat the soul cake in small, careful bites, with the hood still up, and they don't drop a crumb.

They don't say thank you.

Ambrose doesn't wait for it. He's already putting the kettle on.

I lean my corner towards the stool, just a little, the way I lean towards anything new. I want to know what they smell of. Everybody smells of something. Penny smells of pencil shavings and cold tea. Wicker smells of grass and trouble. You smell of your own house, and your soap, and the weather you walked in.

The somebody by the fire smells of nothing at all.

It's like leaning towards a kitchen that isn't there any more.

I close my cover. Not all the way. Enough.

Ambrose brings the tea. While it's cooling, he takes a second soul cake off the tray and bites it, the way a cook always tastes his own batch.

He stops chewing.

He looks at the cake. He looks at the stool. He doesn't say anything, but his jaw goes very still. Later, when the somebody's dozing by the fire, he tells you very quietly what it tasted of.

“Nothing,” he says. “Like eating the shape of a cake.”

The somebody wakes before the tea's gone cold. They turn the hood towards you. I still can't see a face. I can see the fire in two small round places where eyes would be.

“And who are you, that carries a book about?” they say. “What do they call you?”

The kettle ticks. Ambrose has gone very still at the range. In every story I've ever held, there's a moment where somebody asks your name at a fire. I've never liked what happens next.

nodes.title: In the morning
nodes.body:
In the morning the stranger's still on the stool by the fire, asleep, with the hood up and the green coat pulled around them like a tent.

Every pot in the Kitchens has been scrubbed.

All of them. The big stock pots and the little milk pans and the copper ones Ambrose saves for jam. Somebody's scoured them till they shine, and hung them back on their hooks in a perfect row, biggest to smallest, with their handles all pointing the same way.

Ambrose stands in front of them in his nightshirt with a cold cup of tea in his hand. He doesn't say anything for a long time.

Then he says, “That's not how I hang them.”

He doesn't move them back.

storyScenes.title: Three Nights
storyScenes.opening:
The stranger who knocked at the Kitchens' west door on All Souls' Eve has been at the Academy for three nights now. The small one, in the long green coat that's far too big for them.

Nobody's learned their name. The students have started calling them the Guest, with a capital G, the way you'd say the Headmistress or the Weather. The Guest sleeps on the stool by the fire. The Guest eats whatever Ambrose puts in front of them: porridge, stew, toast, the burnt ends of things, a whole apple, core and all. The Guest never says thank you, and never refuses a second helping.

And every morning, every pot in the Kitchens is scrubbed and hung back biggest to smallest, and nobody did it.

Dr. Vellum comes down to the Kitchens on the third evening with a notebook, a thermometer and a look.

“I'd like to examine your visitor,” Vellum says. “Temperature. Pulse. Appetite. Three nights of eating like that and nobody's taken a single measurement.”

Ambrose is chopping onions. He doesn't stop.

“No.”

“It's a simple examination.”

“They've eaten at my hearth three nights,” says Ambrose. “That makes them a guest. You don't poke a guest with a thermometer.”

“That isn't a rule.”

“It's the oldest rule there is.”

Professor Boggle is sitting at the end of the long table, mending a tea towel. She keeps the Academy's rooms. She knows where every key is and which stairs creak and which chimneys need a word. She doesn't look up from her needle.

“He's right, I'm afraid,” she says. “The house rules are older than the Academy. Three nights at the hearth and they're under its roof. Nobody can turn them out. Nobody can harm them. Not till they choose to go.”

Vellum looks at the Guest. The Guest is sitting on the stool by the fire, eating a bowl of porridge very slowly, with the hood up.

“And if they never choose to go?”

Nobody answers that.

Ambrose puts a cup of tea down by Professor Boggle's elbow without asking if she wants one. She says, “Ambrose, that's very kind of—” and he's already gone back to the onions. She finishes the sentence anyway, quietly, to the tea towel. I'm the only one who hears the end of it.

nodes.title: Bonfire Night
nodes.body:
It's Bonfire Night, and the courtyard's full.

The bonfire's taller than the stable roof. It roars and spits, and sparks go up into the black sky like somebody's shaken out a blanket full of stars. Everybody's in scarves. Everybody's breath is showing. Ambrose has brought out trays of parkin, sticky and dark and smelling of black treacle and ginger, and bags of bonfire toffee you have to break with a little hammer.

The Guest stands at the very edge of the firelight.

They won't come closer. Everybody else is crowding in to the warmth, holding their hands out, and the Guest stays back where the dark starts, in their long green coat, with a square of parkin in their clean hands.

Penny finds Ambrose at the toffee table. She's carrying his book.

It's *The Middlemost Cookery*. He bought it at an estate sale thirty years ago and he carries it everywhere, in his apron pocket, wrapped in a tea towel. The spine's held together with string. He won't say what he keeps looking for in it. There's a page at the very back, stuck down under the endpaper, that he's never been able to read. Penny's holding it open at the page for parkin.

“Ambrose. Read the second line.”

He reads it. His face does something slow.

The second line says *1 lb of oatmeal, ½ lb of black _reacle.*

The T's gone. It isn't smudged. It isn't torn. There's just a clean small gap where a letter used to be, like a missing tooth.

“It was there on Sunday,” says Penny. “I checked. I always check.”

Somewhere behind us, in the dark at the edge of the light, the Guest takes another small bite of parkin.

Somebody touches your elbow. It's Professor Momort. He's wrapped in a coat with too many collars, and his face is lit orange on one side by the fire.

“Whatever you do,” he says, very low, “don't thank it. Not for anything. If it does you a kindness, say *I'm grateful*. Never the other thing.”

“Why?”

He looks at the Guest for a long moment.

“Because thanks are payment,” he says. “And you don't know what you'd be paying for.”

Then a rocket goes up with a scream and bursts green over the stables, and when I look back, he's gone.

storyScenes.title: Flat
storyScenes.opening:
It's Martinmas, and the Great Hall's gone very quiet at supper.

There's goose. There's always goose at Martinmas, a big crackling brown one for every table, and red cabbage, and roast potatoes with crunchy edges. It looks wonderful. It smells wonderful. The whole Hall's full of the smell of it, warm and fat and gold.

Nobody can taste it.

You can see it go round the Hall, table by table. Somebody takes a bite and stops chewing. Somebody else frowns at a potato as if it's told a lie. A first-year puts down his fork and says, loudly, “Is it me?”

It isn't him. It's everybody.

Pippa stands up on her bench.

“It's the punctuation,” she says. “Somebody's taken the full stop off the gravy. Gravy without a full stop just goes *on.*”

Nobody laughs. That's how I know it's bad.

It's been ten days since the Guest came. I've been counting. The Guest's the stranger in the green coat who knocked at the Kitchens' west door on All Souls' Eve, and Ambrose fed it, and it never left. It sleeps on the stool by the Kitchens fire. Every night every pot in the house gets scrubbed, and nobody owns up. At first everybody said *them*. Now everybody says *it*. I don't know when that changed.

And nobody thanks it. Not for anything. Professor Momort says thanks are a kind of payment, and you don't know what you'd be paying for. So when it fills your glass, you say nothing. Or you say *I'm grateful*. Never the other thing.

At the end of the Hall, by the door to the Kitchens, the Guest is going round the tables with a big jug of water, filling up glasses. Nobody asked it to. At every place, it stops for just a moment, and leans a little over the plate, the way you'd lean over a flower.

Then it moves on. And the next plate goes flat.

Serenity's sitting near the window. She's got a plate of goose in front of her and she hasn't touched it. She's watching the Hall. And then she starts to laugh.

It's a surprised laugh. It comes out of her before she can stop it, bright and sudden, like a bird getting out of a box.

Everybody turns to look.

“Sorry,” she says. “Sorry. It's just—” She picks up her fork. She puts down her fork. “Now you know.”

“Know what?” says Pippa.

“What it's like.” Serenity pushes her plate away an inch. “I haven't tasted anything since October. Not since the Count. It all tastes like paper. I've been eating paper for six weeks and smiling about it.”

The Hall's quieter than I've ever heard it. Even the fire's listening.

nodes.title: Martinmas bread
nodes.body:
Later, in the Kitchens, Ambrose is halving loaves.

It's a Martinmas thing. Saint Martin was a soldier, in the old story, who met a beggar at a gate on a freezing night and cut his own cloak in two with his sword to share it. So at Martinmas Ambrose cuts every loaf in half, and keeps one half, and puts the other half in a basket by the door, for whoever needs it.

He cuts one more than usual. He takes the extra half over to the stool by the fire and puts it in the Guest's clean hands.

The Guest eats it. Ambrose watches.

*The Middlemost Cookery*'s on the dresser, wrapped in its tea towel. That's Ambrose's old cookbook. Since Bonfire Night, letters have been going out of it, one at a time. They don't fall out. They leave. Ambrose doesn't open it in front of people any more.

Serenity's come down too. She's sitting on the end of the long table with her boots swinging, the way she sits on everything, and she's watching the Guest as well. You've set me down beside her.

“It does it to every plate,” she says, quietly. “Have you seen? It leans over. Like it's smelling them. And then they're gone.”

I'd tell her she's right, if I could tell her things. I can't. I press my corner against her map case instead, and she looks down at me, and then at the Guest.

Because it's true. The Guest went round every place in the Hall. It leaned over every plate. When it got to Serenity's, it leaned, and stopped, and its hood turned up towards her face for a long moment.

Then it moved on. There was nothing on her plate for it to take.

Serenity turns her mug of tea round and round in her hands.

“It looked at me,” she says. “Like I was a jar it couldn't get the lid off.”

storyScenes.title: The Rescue
storyScenes.opening:
Penny's been up all night with *The Middlemost Cookery*.

That's Ambrose's cookbook. He bought it at an estate sale thirty years ago, and he's carried it in his apron pocket ever since, wrapped in a tea towel. On Bonfire Night Penny found the first letter gone out of it: the T in *treacle*. It wasn't smudged. It wasn't torn. It was just gone.

She's got it open on the long table, with a lamp on each side and a magnifying glass and a stack of index cards a hand high. She's gone through it page by page and written down every missing letter. Her eyes are red. Her pencil's worn to a stub.

“Two hundred and fourteen,” she says. “Since Bonfire Night. The S's are going fastest. Then the E's. The Christmas pudding's lost all its spices. The gingerbread's lost its *bread.*” She doesn't look at the stool by the fire when she says the next bit. “The first one went four days after the Guest came.”

Ambrose stands at her shoulder. He's gone grey under his kitchen colour.

“Thirty years,” he says. “I've had that book thirty years.”

“There's something else.” Penny turns the pages back. “Look. Stone soup.”

The stone soup page is whole. Every letter's there, crisp and black. *Put a clean stone in the pot. Tell everybody you're making soup.*

“You made it on Thursday,” says Penny. “For the second-years. And the soda bread, there, you made on Tuesday. And the leek and potato. All whole.”

She sits back. She looks at Ambrose the way she looks at a piece of evidence that's finally decided to speak.

“The only recipes keeping their letters,” she says, “are the ones somebody's making.”

The Kitchens go very quiet. By the fire, the Guest's scrubbing a pan that's already clean, in its green coat, with its sleeves rolled up four times.

Ambrose ties his apron tighter.

“Then we cook,” he says.

nodes.title: Everybody cooks
nodes.body:
It's chaos.

There are second-years making scones you could build a wall with. There's a boy from the Glint Hall crying over an onion, and he isn't sad, it's just the onion. Professor Boggle's making soda bread with her sleeves pushed up to the elbow and flour in her eyebrows. Pippa's going round correcting the recipe cards. “A *pinch*,” she's telling a first-year, “is not a measurement. It's a threat.”

Ambrose stands in the middle of it all with a wooden spoon, saying “Lower the heat. Lower. Lower. Good,” to everyone at once.

And Wicker Eddies is making an omelette.

He's never made an omelette. He's never made anything, as far as I know, unless you count trouble. He's got the pan far too hot and he's got eggshell in it and he's frowning at it with the most serious face I've ever seen him wear. He doesn't look at Serenity, at the far end of the table. He looks at the pan as if the pan is a dare.

When it's done, it's brown on one side and runny on the other. He puts it on a plate. He walks it down the whole length of the long table and sets it down in front of her, and walks away again before she can say anything.

Serenity looks at the omelette. She takes a bite. She can't taste it. Everybody knows she can't.

She eats the whole thing anyway, slowly, without a word.

Soren's at the dresser, doing something nobody else has noticed. He's laying out teaspoons. Each one's got a tiny taste on it: a grain of sea salt, a drop of honey, a curl of lemon peel, a smear of mustard, a single blackcurrant. Beside each spoon there's a folded paper slip with a number on it, one to nine.

When Serenity gets up to put her plate away, the first slip's sitting on her map case. It says, in Soren's small careful hand: *Start at the dresser. Go in order. Don't skip seven.*

She stands there holding it. She doesn't open the rest. But she puts it in her pocket.

nodes.title: What do you need?
nodes.body:
At the end of the afternoon, when the Kitchens have gone quiet and sticky, Min-seo Kim does something nobody else has thought to do.

She goes and sits on the floor by the stool, beside the Guest. Not too close. Close enough.

“Can I ask you something?”

The hood turns.

“You've been here two weeks. Everybody's been talking about you. Nobody's asked you anything.” She pulls her knees up. “What do you need?”

The Guest is quiet for a long time. The fire ticks. I'm holding my breath, as much as a book can.

“Something I used to have,” it says, at last.

“What was it?”

“I don't remember.” The clean hands turn over, palms up, empty. “That's why I'm eating. I'm looking for it. I think it tasted of this house.”

Then Ambrose turns round from the range, and looks at you.

“Your kitchen counts too,” he says. “Whatever you make out there, where you live. It counts. A recipe's only alive while somebody's making it. So make something.”

storyScenes.title: The Offer
storyScenes.opening:
Serenity comes down to the Kitchens at three in the morning.

She does that now. Since October, she hears things at night. Pages turning in the walls. Doors that are really books. She can't sleep through it, so she walks, and her walks end up here, where it's warm.

Ambrose has left something out for her. He always does now. Tonight it's a bowl of leek and potato soup under a plate, on the warm corner of the range, and a spoon laid next to it, and a folded napkin. He doesn't say anything about it in the mornings. She doesn't either.

Penny's card's on the Kitchen door behind her, *Missing* and *Restored*. In this light I can't read the numbers. I don't need to. The first one's bigger.

You're there because you couldn't sleep either. You're sitting on the bench by the dresser with me on your knees. I've got my leaves shut. I keep them shut after dark now.

The Guest is awake.

It's at the sink, in its long green coat, scrubbing a pot. The pot's already clean. It scrubs it anyway, slowly, round and round, the way you'd stroke a dog. In the low light from the range, I can see that the sleeves of the coat are far too long for it. It's rolled them up four times.

Serenity sits down with her soup. She can't taste it. She hasn't tasted anything since October, since the Count. She eats it anyway.

The Guest stops scrubbing.

“I could give it back,” it says.

Serenity's spoon stops halfway.

“The taste of things.” The Guest doesn't turn round. It talks to the pot. “Soup. Rain. All of it. I know where it went. I've been eating everybody else's. I could give you yours.”

It's very quiet. Even the walls have stopped turning pages.

At night the Guest doesn't smell of nothing any more. It smells of frost. Frost and old iron, like a gate in winter. I didn't notice it till now. I wish I hadn't.

“What for?” says Serenity.

Now it turns. The hood tilts towards her.

“One evening,” it says. “You've got one I'd like. An evening in November.”

{october-evening}

Serenity looks down at her soup. She stirs it. She can't taste it. She hasn't tasted anything for seven weeks.

Then she looks at you.

{why-you}

“What would you do?”

storyScenes.title: Stir-up Sunday
storyScenes.opening:
It's Stir-up Sunday, the last Sunday before Advent, and the whole Academy's queueing out of the Kitchens and halfway up the stairs.

That's the custom. Ambrose makes the Christmas pudding today, in the biggest bowl in the building, a great brown earthenware one he can barely lift. And everybody in the house has to take a turn at the stirring. You stir from east to west, the way the three kings travelled in the old story. You shut your eyes. And you make a wish, and you don't say it out loud, or it won't come.

Ever since the Guest came, letters have been going out of Ambrose's old cookbook, *The Middlemost Cookery*. A recipe only keeps its letters while somebody's making it, so the whole Academy's been cooking. The pudding page has got its spices back, letter by letter. Penny's count is on the Kitchen door, *Missing* and *Restored*, and the second column keeps going up. Some of the letters came from out there, from people's own kitchens, and Ambrose says that's the strangest and best part.

The queue moves. Pippa stirs and wishes with her whole face screwed up. Dr. Vellum stirs exactly three times and makes a note. Serenity stirs, and laughs at something, and won't say what.

You stir. I can't stir. But you hold me over the bowl while you do it, and I make a wish too. I'm not telling you what it is either. Those are the rules.

Then the Guest steps up, in its green coat, off the stool by the fire where it's slept every night since All Souls.

Nobody's sure it's allowed. Everybody looks at Ambrose. Ambrose holds out the wooden spoon.

The Guest takes it in both its clean hands. It stirs from east to west, slowly, round and round. It shuts its eyes, under the hood.

And then it does what you must never do. It says its wish out loud.

“Home,” it says. “The smell of the house when the bowl was put down. I want to go home.”

The spoon stops.

At the back of the Kitchens, in the doorway to the stairs, there's a tall dark shape in a long black coat. It's Headmistress Thorne. I didn't hear her come. She's standing perfectly still with her hands folded, and she's watching the Guest, and her face is doing nothing at all.

Then she turns and goes back up the stairs, and doesn't come into the room.

She hasn't come into a room the Guest's been in all month. I've only just noticed.

nodes.title: Under the endpaper
nodes.body:
That night, after the queue's gone and the pudding's steaming in its cloth, Ambrose sits down at the long table with *The Middlemost Cookery*.

He doesn't open it at a recipe. He opens it at the back, at the place he always opens it, where the endpaper's coming loose. For thirty years he's been trying to read what's under that endpaper. There's a page stuck to it, with writing nobody's ever been able to make out.

Tonight you can read it.

Not all of it. The Academy's cooking has brought back most of the letters. The title's whole now, in old brown handwriting:

*A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.*

Under it there's a list of things. Most of it's there. Some of it isn't. There are gaps, like missing teeth.

Ambrose reads it three times. Then he lays his hand flat on the page, the way you'd lay your hand on a sleeping animal to feel it breathe.

“That's it,” he says. “That's what I've been looking for.”

He looks across at the stool by the fire. The Guest's asleep there, in its green coat, with its sleeves rolled up four times.

“It was never for us,” he says. “It's for them. It always was.”

storyScenes.title: A Place at the Table
storyScenes.opening:
Tonight everybody's eating in the Kitchens.

Not in the Great Hall. Ambrose wanted the long table, so the long table's what they've got. It's been scrubbed white. It's set end to end with every plate in the building, odd ones and good ones, blue-rimmed and plain, and candles stuck in saucers all the way down the middle. There's soup. There's a ham. There's mashed potato in a bowl the size of a well. There's the cranberry sauce Penny made. It's set too hard and has to be cut with a knife, and it's perfect.

And there's one chair at the top of the table that nobody's sitting in.

It's got a plate in front of it. A full one. Soup and ham and potato and a spoonful of the cranberry. A candle. A napkin folded into a little hat.

Nobody sits in it. Nobody asks about it either. Everybody seems to know.

Ambrose stands up at the end, with his apron still on.

“That one's for whoever's missing,” he says. “Everybody's got somebody. Somebody who used to sit at your table and doesn't now. They get a place too. That's all.” He sits down. “Eat your soup.”

Everyone eats their soup.

It tastes of soup. It tastes of leeks and pepper and good stock. All month the Guest's leaned over people's plates and breathed in, and afterwards there was nothing left in them to taste. The Academy's been cooking against it for two weeks. Tonight the Guest hasn't leaned over a single plate. It's sitting halfway down the table on a bench between Penny and a second-year, eating ham. It's eating it the ordinary way. It's tasting it, as far as I can tell.

I've been watching it all evening. I've never seen it look so much like it belongs somewhere.

Down at the far end, the talk goes quiet and low.

Penny says she'd set the chair for her grandmother, who taught her to file things alphabetically and to always check twice. Wicker doesn't say who he'd set it for. He looks at the chair for a long time and then cuts himself more ham. Soren says, “My father. He used to fold the napkins like that,” and touches the little hat on the empty plate, very gently, and puts it back exactly.

Serenity's sitting between Wicker and Soren. That's an accident, I think. Or it isn't. The table's very long, and she's got a lot of room on either side, and she's chosen the middle.

Professor Boggle keeps the Academy's rooms. She's been trying to thank Ambrose for twenty years. For the soup when she was ill. For the cake on her fiftieth. For a thousand cups of tea put down by her elbow without a word. Every time, he's walked off before she got to the end of the sentence.

Tonight she gets up and goes round to the range, where he's ladling seconds.

“Ambrose. I'm grateful,” she says.

He stops ladling.

They're the right words. They're the old words, the ones Professor Momort's been telling everybody to use all month. They don't pay him, and they don't send him away. They just sit there between the two of them, in the steam, like a warm plate.

He doesn't walk off. He doesn't say anything either. But he stands there and lets her have said it.

That's new.

storyScenes.title: The Bowl
storyScenes.opening:
It's the last day of November and Ambrose is cooking something small.

All month the Kitchens have been loud. Today they're quiet. He's sent everybody out. There's just him at the range, and the Guest asleep on its stool by the fire, and Serenity on the end of the long table, swinging her boots, and you, with me open on your knees. I've opened my leaves for this. I want to see.

*The Middlemost Cookery*'s propped against the bread crock, open at the back, at the page he looked for for thirty years. It came clear on Stir-up Sunday: *A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.* Ambrose has read the page so many times he doesn't need to. He reads it anyway.

It isn't a feast. That's the first surprise. After thirty years I thought it'd be a feast. It's oats. It's a small pan of oats, cooked slowly in milk, stirred the whole time with the handle of a wooden spoon. A pinch of salt. Pippa isn't here to object. When it's thick, a spoonful of honey on top, and a knob of butter melting into a little gold pool, and a splash of cream poured round the edge, cold, so it doesn't mix.

That's all.

He takes down a bowl. It's a plain brown one from the very back of the dresser, chipped on one side, older than anything else in the room. I've never seen him use it.

He fills it. He doesn't put a spoon in.

Then he carries it across the Kitchens, and he doesn't put it in the Guest's hands. He kneels down and puts it on the hearth, on the warm stones, beside the stool. And he gets up and goes back to the range, and turns his back, and starts washing the pan.

He doesn't say who it's for.

Everybody knows.

The Guest wakes.

It looks at the bowl for a long time. Then it slides off the stool and kneels by the hearth, and pushes back its hood.

I can see its face now, for the first time. It's small and brown and creased like a walnut, with a big soft nose and two bright black eyes, and it looks very, very old, and very, very tired.

It leans over the bowl. It breathes in.

*The Middlemost Cookery*'s propped against the bread crock, open at the back, at the page he looked for for thirty years. It came clear on Stir-up Sunday: *A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.* Ambrose has read the page so many times he doesn't need to. He reads it anyway.

It isn't a feast. That's the first surprise. After thirty years I thought it'd be a feast. It's oats. It's a small pan of oats, cooked slowly in milk, stirred the whole time with the handle of a wooden spoon. A pinch of salt. Pippa isn't here to object. When it's thick, a spoonful of honey on top, and a knob of butter melting into a little gold pool, and a splash of cream poured round the edge, cold, so it doesn't mix.

That's all.

He takes down a bowl. It's a plain brown one from the very back of the dresser, chipped on one side, older than anything else in the room. I've never seen him use it.

He fills it. He doesn't put a spoon in.

Then he carries it across the Kitchens, and he doesn't put it in the Guest's hands. He kneels down and puts it on the hearth, on the warm stones, beside the stool. And he gets up and goes back to the range, and turns his back, and starts washing the pan.

He doesn't say who it's for.

Everybody knows.

The Guest wakes.

It looks at the bowl for a long time. Then it slides off the stool and kneels by the hearth, and pushes back its hood.

I can see its face now, for the first time. It's small and brown and creased like a walnut, with a big soft nose and two bright black eyes, and it looks very, very old, and very, very tired.

It leans over the bowl. It breathes in.

nodes.title: It smells like home
nodes.body:
The smell of the oats goes all through the Kitchens. Honey and warm milk and butter going brown. It's the plainest smell in the world. It's the smell of a house at night when everyone's in bed and somebody's left something warm out for whoever needs it.

The Guest picks up the bowl in both its clean hands, and drinks from the side, the old way, with no spoon.

And it changes.

Not much. Nothing like a story where someone turns into a swan. The green coat goes on being a green coat, too big. But the frost goes out of the room. The old iron smell goes out of it. The Guest smells of something at last. It smells of oats and soot and soap and a warm brick floor. It smells like the Kitchens.

It smells like it's home.

It sets the bowl down, empty. It looks round the Kitchens at the pots, and the long table, and the range, and Ambrose's back, still turned, still washing the pan that's already clean.

Then it looks at you.

“I could go,” it says. “I know the way now. I can taste it.” It touches the brown bowl. “Or I could stay. Keep the pots. Like before. If the house would have me.”

*Like before.* So it's been here before. It kept the pots in these Kitchens a long time ago, before anybody now was born. I think I've known since the first morning.

Behind it, very faintly, I can smell frost again. Far off. Out past the west door. Something out there's waiting to see what it chooses. Something that's had everybody's suppers, all month.

It looks at Ambrose's back. It looks at you. It looks, for a long moment, at the brown bowl on the hearth.

“I'm grateful,” it says.

It's the only right thing to say. It doesn't pay anyone. It doesn't send anyone away. It's just true. Then it's gone, into the dark, and the door swings shut on its own.

nodes.title: Finished
nodes.body:
When it's over, Serenity gets down off the table.

She goes over to the range, where Ambrose is still washing the pan. She doesn't touch him. She leans against the warm brick beside him.

“That was a good bowl,” she says.

He doesn't answer. He keeps washing.

“Ambrose. I'm grateful. For the soup. Every night. You never said and I never said and I want to say it properly.”

He stops washing. He stands there with his hands in the water.

And for the first time in thirty years, Ambrose Trencher lets somebody finish thanking him.

Later, when the Kitchens have gone dark, Professor Boggle comes down the back stairs with a plate under a cloth. She's cooked for him. Cheese on toast, a little burnt at the corners. She puts it down in front of him and doesn't say a word, the way he never does.

Ambrose looks at it for a long time. Then he sits down, which nobody's ever seen him do in his own kitchen, and eats every bite.

storyScenes.title: The Pot Watch
storyScenes.opening:
Wicker's decided to catch whoever scrubs the pots.

It's been a week since the Guest came. That's the stranger in the long green coat who knocked at the Kitchens' west door on All Souls' Eve, and ate a soul cake by the fire, and never left. Every morning since, somebody's scrubbed every pot in the Kitchens and hung it back on its hook, biggest to smallest, handles all one way. Ambrose didn't do it. Nobody did it. That's what everybody says. Wicker says nobody isn't a person, and he's going to see their face.

So it's eleven at night, and the three of you are under the long table with a blanket and a bag of bonfire toffee left over from Thursday. You, and Wicker, and Soren, who says he's only come to stop Wicker doing anything stupid. I'm on your knees. My leaves are shut. I keep them shut after dark now.

The fire's banked down to a red heap. The Guest's asleep on its stool beside it, with the hood up and the sleeves of the coat rolled four times, and its clean hands folded in its lap. It doesn't move. I don't think it's breathing. I don't want to check.

“If it's the Guest,” Wicker whispers, “I'm going to say thanks. Just to see what happens.”

“Don't,” says Soren. “Momort said. Never thank it.”

“Momort says loads of things.”

“He said that one plainly. He never says anything plainly.”

Wicker eats a piece of toffee very loudly. That means Soren's won.

At midnight Soren's asleep sitting up, with his chin on his chest. At one, Wicker's asleep with his mouth open, holding the toffee hammer.

At three, the scrubbing starts.

It's a small sound. Round and round. A pot hums when it's being scrubbed. I didn't know that. And under the pot's humming there's another hum, very low, with no words in it. It's an old tune. I don't know its name. I think it knows mine.

You're the only one awake. You and me.

storyScenes.title: Salt
storyScenes.opening:
Ambrose has salted the stock three times, and it's still not right.

He stands at the range with the big stock pot, tasting off the end of a wooden spoon. He frowns. He adds a pinch. He tastes. He adds another. He's been the Academy's cook for thirty years. He doesn't salt twice. I've never seen him do it.

“It isn't the salt,” says Dr. Vellum.

Dr. Vellum's at the end of the long table with her notebook, a thermometer, the brass kitchen scales and six first-years. Every first-year's got a cup of the stock and a pencil and a card that says, at the top, *TASTE, 1 TO 10.*

Vellum isn't allowed to examine the Guest. That's the stranger in the green coat who knocked at the west door on All Souls and has slept on the stool by the fire ever since. Ambrose said no, on the third night. Professor Boggle said the house said no too: once somebody's eaten at your hearth three nights they're a guest, and nobody pokes a guest. So Vellum's examining the soup instead.

“Same bones,” she says, reading out of her notebook. “Same weight of salt. Same onions. I weighed them. Same temperature, to the degree. And every night since Thursday it scores lower.” She holds up the cards. “Tonight's average is four. One of them's written, *Tastes like soup somebody told me about.*”

“Food's fuel,” says Ambrose, without turning round. “You've always said so. So why do you care what it tastes of?”

Vellum opens her mouth. She shuts it again. She writes something down and doesn't show anybody.

I know this. I know it from somewhere. Everything going a bit less every day, so slowly that nobody says anything till it's gone. I hate it. I hate it more than anything there is.

On the stool by the fire the Guest's eating a bowl of the same stock, slowly, with the hood up. It's the only one in the Kitchens who's asked for seconds.

storyScenes.title: Nine Spoons
storyScenes.opening:
It's past midnight, and Serenity's laying nine teaspoons out on the dresser in the Kitchens, in a row.

They're Soren's. He laid them out on the afternoon the whole Academy cooked, each with a tiny taste on it and a folded paper slip beside it, numbered one to nine. Serenity only took the first slip. It says: *Start at the dresser. Go in order. Don't skip seven.* She's carried it round in her pocket ever since.

In the morning the spoons were washed and back in the drawer. Everything in the Kitchens gets washed in the night, and nobody does it. And the other eight slips had gone. Nobody knows where.

So she's doing it again herself, from memory. She looked at them very hard that afternoon. She's good at remembering where things go. That's what maps are. Sea salt on one. Honey on two. Lemon peel, mustard, one blackcurrant, a fleck of black pepper. She puts them on, one by one.

Then she gets to seven, and stops.

“I can't remember seven,” she says. “I think it was empty. Why would he leave one empty?”

She leaves it empty. She does eight and nine: a shred of mint, one grain of sugar.

The trouble is, Serenity can't taste. She hasn't since October, since the Count. Everything tastes of paper to her. And this month the rest of the Academy's food's been going the same way, ever since the Guest came. The Guest's asleep right now on its stool by the fire, in its green coat, with its sleeves rolled up four times.

So nine tastes on nine spoons is either a very kind thing or a very stupid one. Serenity's trying to work out which. She's been trying for ten minutes.

You're here because you couldn't sleep. You've got me under your arm.

“Will you do them with me?” she says. “I'll eat them. You tell me what they're like. Properly. Like you're telling somebody who's never had them.”

That's a job. I love it when somebody gives you a job.

nodes.title: One to seven
nodes.body:
Spoon one's a grain of sea salt. She eats it. You tell her it's a spark on your tongue. It's the sea when a wave smacks you in the face. She's drawn the sea a hundred times. Now she knows what it's like.

Spoon two's honey. You tell her it's slow, and it's a summer afternoon, and it sticks to the back of everything. Three's lemon peel, and you tell her it's loud and it's yellow. Four's mustard, and you tell her it goes up your nose and shouts. Five's one blackcurrant, and you tell her it's purple. Purple isn't a taste. Except it is.

She eats every one. She can't taste any of them. She listens to you with her eyes shut, very hard.

Six is the pepper. It makes her sneeze, and she laughs, because a sneeze is something.

Then seven.

Spoon seven's empty. There's nothing on it at all. It's clean and cold, and there's no slip to say what it's for. She's had nothing on her tongue since October. And Soren put a spoon of it in the row and told her not to skip it.

By the fire, the Guest's hood turns towards the dresser. It's awake. I don't know how long it's been awake.

nodes.body:

Wicker's left something on the dresser too. It's a recipe card, pinned down with a fork, in letters an inch high: *OMELETTE (FIXED). Less hot. No shells. More nerve.*

It doesn't say who it's for.

storyScenes.title: The Tray
storyScenes.opening:
Every night at seven Ambrose sends a tray up to the Headmistress.

He's done it for thirty years. Soup, bread, a bit of whatever's on, a pot of tea, and a cloth over the top. Headmistress Thorne eats in her study at the top of the tower, on her own. She's never once eaten in the Kitchens. Ambrose used to say that was manners.

This month the tray's been coming back untouched.

Every night. The soup cold, the bread whole, the cloth still folded. Ambrose doesn't say anything about it. He scrapes it into the pig bucket and looks at the stool by the fire, where the Guest's sitting in its green coat, eating its second helping. It's been on that stool since All Souls. Seventeen days. I've been counting.

Tonight Ambrose gives the tray to you.

“Take it up,” he says. “She'll open the door to a student. She won't to me, this month.”

So you're on the back stairs with the tray, and me under your arm, going up. The stairs go round and round. The soup's getting cold. That's a waste, because tonight it nearly tastes of soup.

Halfway up, you stop.

There's somebody on the stairs below you. Coming up behind, very quietly.

It's the Guest.

It's never left the Kitchens. Not once. It stops two steps below you and looks up the stairwell with its hood tipped back, at the dark at the top, where the Headmistress's door is.

Then the door at the top opens, and Thorne's standing in it.

nodes.body:
Thorne comes down three steps. She's tall and dark, in her long black coat, and she stops with the tray between her and the Guest. She doesn't look at the tray. She looks past you, down at the hood.

The Guest bows. It bows low. Lower than anybody bows at the Academy. It's the bow out of an old story, where the one bowing's been told exactly how low to go.

Thorne doesn't bow back.

The Guest straightens up. It looks at her for a long moment. Then it goes back down, round and round, without a sound, and it's gone.

Thorne lifts the cloth off the tray. She looks at the soup. She puts the cloth back.

storyScenes.title: Letters Coming Home
storyScenes.opening:
Penny's found something odd about the letters coming back.

All month, letters have been going out of *The Middlemost Cookery*, Ambrose's old cookbook. They started going on Bonfire Night, four days after the Guest came, and they only come back when somebody makes the recipe. So the Academy's been cooking, all of it, for more than a week. On the Kitchen door Penny's card says *Missing* and *Restored*, and the second number keeps going up.

Penny's got the Cookery open on the long table under two lamps. Pippa's on the bench beside her with a magnifying glass the size of a saucer. Pippa Pilcrow cares about letters more than anybody alive. She says they're the only people who never let you down.

“Look,” says Penny. “The ones that went missing were all the same. Brown ink. Somebody's neat handwriting, a hundred years old. Now look what's come back.”

You look.

The soda bread's whole again. But the second E in *soda* is round and fat and blue. It's biro. The S in *scones* has come back in thick pencil, pressed hard, the way a little kid writes. The pudding page has got a T in some grandmother's curly copperplate, with a loop on the top like a hat.

“They come back in the hand of whoever made it,” says Penny. “Every one. I've checked forty.”

Pippa's nose is an inch off the page. “That's a lefty,” she says. “Look at the slope. That one was in a hurry. And that one,” she points at a careful little R, “was somebody who'd never cooked before in their life and was scared stiff.”

Ambrose is standing behind them with a tea towel over his shoulder. He hasn't said anything. He's looking at the book. It's full of people now.

Some of the letters aren't from the Academy at all. Penny's sure. They're from out there, from people's own kitchens, wherever those are.

By the fire, the Guest's asleep on its stool in its green coat, with its clean hands open in its lap.

storyScenes.title: The Day-Book
storyScenes.opening:
It's nearly the end of November, and Ambrose can't sleep.

He's at the long table with *The Middlemost Cookery* open at the back, at the page that came clear on Stir-up Sunday: *A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.* For thirty years he's tried to read that page. Now he nearly can. The letters have come home from everybody's cooking, here and out there. All but one line at the very bottom. There's still a gap in it, as long as a few words.

He's going to cook it on the last day. He's decided. He just doesn't know how it ends.

Over by the fire the Guest's asleep on its stool. It's been there since All Souls, in its long green coat with the brass buttons and its sleeves rolled up four times. Four weeks of scrubbed pots. Four weeks of leaning over people's suppers until there was nothing left in them to taste, and then the whole Academy cooking to get it back.

Then Professor Boggle comes down the back stairs in her dressing gown with a book under her arm.

It's huge. It's bound in brown leather gone soft as a glove, and it smells of a hundred years of candle smoke. It's very old and it doesn't say hello. I like it straight away.

“The house day-book,” she says. “The Academy's household accounts, from before. I keep the rooms, so I keep the rooms' books. I've been looking for this in the Pantry drawers all month. It was behind the jam.”

She puts it on the table beside the Cookery and opens it at a page she's marked with a hair ribbon.

nodes.title: The pots not done
nodes.body:
It's a list, in old brown ink. It's the same brown ink as the Cookery. One line a day, every day, all the way down the page.

*Bread, 40 loaves. Candles, 2 doz. Cream, a bowl, for the hearth.*

*Bread, 40 loaves. Coal. Cream, a bowl, for the hearth.*

*Cream, a bowl, for the hearth.*

Every night. For pages and pages. Somebody put a bowl of cream on the hearth every night and wrote it down, and never wrote who it was for. Everybody knew.

Boggle turns the page.

*Paid to the tailor, for a coat for the one that keeps the pots. Green, with brass buttons. As thanks.*

Then the next line: *The pots not done.*

And the next: *The pots not done.*

Then a whole page of it. *The pots not done. The pots not done.* After that the bowl of cream isn't written down any more.

Nobody says anything. Ambrose looks at the stool by the fire. Boggle looks at the stool by the fire. I look too, through the gap in my leaves, at the long green coat and its brass buttons. I count them. I don't know why. I want to know how many there are.

“Thanks are payment,” says Boggle, very quietly. “Momort says it. The house rules say it. Thank the ones who keep a house and you've paid them off, and once they're paid they've got to go.” She puts her finger beside the line about the coat. She doesn't touch it. “Somebody meant it kindly. They gave it a good coat.”

“It doesn't say,” says Boggle. “The day-book's for bread and candles.”

She shuts it, very carefully.

“My grandmother kept the rooms before me,” she says. “She used to say a thing that keeps a house, sent off hungry, doesn't go anywhere good. It goes somewhere cold. Somewhere that'll feed it, and want feeding back.”

Out past the west door, the frost ticks on the iron. I hear it. I don't think they do.

There it is. On the night before the coat, the cream's written down differently. *Oats in milk, a pinch of salt, honey, butter. Cold cream round the edge, poured last. Set on the hearth. No spoon.*

It's the bottom line of the bowl page, word for word. While you're looking, the gap in the Cookery fills itself in, letter by letter, in brown. It's been waiting a very long time to finish that sentence.

nodes.title: The west door
nodes.body:
Before you go up, you look at the west door.

There's frost on the inside of it, all over the iron studs, thick as sugar. It's in the keyhole. It's on the bolts that are painted over so thick they look like knuckles. On the other side of the door, out in the dark, something's standing very still, waiting for the last day.

The Guest sleeps through all of it, in its green coat, by the fire.

In the morning the frost's gone. The pots are scrubbed.

nodes.title: The first of December
nodes.body:
It's the first of December, and the Kitchens are pretending nothing happened.

They're good at it. Ambrose has chalked the menu on the board by the door. It says *Porridge*, and underneath, smaller, *It's cold. Wear the other socks.* The range is lit. The long table's been scrubbed so hard that the knot in the pine has come up pale. Everything's back where it goes.

But I can smell November in the corners. Nutmeg in the cracks of the floor. Burnt sugar from Bonfire Night, still stuck to the underside of the toffee tray. And under all of it, where you'd only notice if you were made of paper, a little cold. Not frost. The memory of frost. The way a step remembers somebody who stood on it a long time.

{november-ending}

Penny's put the white bowl on a shelf in the Record room, under a card that says *Unattributed*, with the black thorn laid inside it. She's tied the thorn down with thread. She says that's for filing reasons.

I think it's so it can't get out.

options.line:
The pots are done.

That's the first thing I see. They're hanging in their row over the range, biggest to smallest, every handle pointing the same way, shining like somebody had all night and nothing better to do. Which somebody did.

The stool's still by the fire. Nobody's on it. The brown bowl's on the hearth, washed and dry and empty, waiting for tonight.

Wicker comes in for porridge. He's learning to cook now, badly, on purpose, every day. He sees the pots, and his face does something soft, and he opens his mouth and says, “Oh, that's—tha—”

Min-seo's behind him in the queue. She puts her whole hand over his mouth before he can finish.

He looks at her over her fingers. She doesn't take it away.

“You don't,” she says. “Not to it. Say you're grateful, if you've got to say something. Or do the washing up.”

Wicker does the washing up. He's terrible at it. Something in the dark beside the range watches him do it, I think, and doesn't say a word, the way you don't say anything to somebody who's trying.

His name's Aiken Drum. He told us, at the end. I'm calling him he now, because a thing with a name is a somebody.

There's an old song from Galloway, in Scotland, about a brownie called Aiken Drum, who worked a farm all night for a bowl of brose and went away when somebody gave him a pair of trousers. That part's folklore. It's real folklore. You can look it up. I don't know if it's the same Aiken Drum. I haven't asked. You don't ask.

The stool's gone from beside the fire.

Not moved. Gone. Ambrose has put it in the Pantry, behind the flour sacks, where he doesn't have to look at it. He hasn't said a thing about it. He's said a great deal about porridge.

The pots are hanging over the range in no order at all. Ambrose did them himself last night, the way he's always done them, fast and loud and wrong. One of the little ones is upside down. He keeps looking at it. He hasn't fixed it.

There was something on the west step this morning: a brass button, tarnished, with a loop of green thread still through it. Just one. Very clean. Ambrose picked it up and didn't say anything, and now it's in his apron pocket. I can hear it clink when he stirs.

It's gone home. Wherever home is, for something like that. The first place, before there were kitchens. I don't know where it is. I only know the frost hasn't come in under the west door since. Not once. The onions have stopped being needed, and Ambrose keeps forgetting, and moving them back anyway.

The west door's shut. Ambrose has pushed the sack of onions back against it, and then, after he'd thought about it, a second sack.

The pots are hanging in no order at all.

*The Middlemost Cookery*'s on the dresser, open, and I can see the gaps in it from here. Small clean holes in the lines where the letters went, like a smile with teeth out. They didn't come back. They went with it, out into the cold, to wherever the Court sits down to eat.

Ambrose doesn't look at the gaps. He's making porridge, a huge pot of it, enough for everybody twice. He makes everything like that. Too much, for whoever turns up.

“Keep cooking,” he says, to nobody, stirring. “Somebody should.”

He's put a stool back by the fire. Nobody's on it. I don't think he expects anybody to be. I think he just can't stand the space where it was.

recalls.fallback:
November ended on the last night, at the hearth. Ambrose cooked one small plain bowl from the back of the Cookery and set it down by the fire without saying who it was for. What happened after that is the Kitchens' business, and they're keeping it.

The stool's still by the fire. The cold's still under the west door, a little, if you know where to stand.

nodes.title: The long nights
nodes.body:
{serenity-at-breakfast}

The nights are getting long now. Every evening the dark comes in a bit earlier and stays a bit later, like it's decided to move in. Yesterday Ambrose looked at the window at four o'clock and it was already black. He said, to nobody, “Somebody'll have to sit up with that.”

He meant the dark. I think. He doesn't say what he means. He makes porridge about it.

But he looked at you when he said it.

options.line:
Serenity comes down to breakfast and eats three bowls of porridge with golden syrup, and then a fourth, because she can. She tastes everything now. She licks the syrup spoon. She puts a pinch of salt on her tongue just to feel it go off like a firework.

Sometimes somebody mentions the evening, the one in November that she gave away, and she gets a polite, puzzled look and says, “Tell me again.”

So they do. They take turns. Everybody who was there has their own bit of it, and they hand it to her like a dish passed down the table. She listens like it's a story about somebody she'd have liked.

Serenity comes down to breakfast and eats her porridge, which still tastes of paper. She minds it less than she did. She's started doing a thing: she gets whoever's next to her to tell her what it tastes like, and she eats while they talk.

This morning it's Penny. “Oats,” says Penny, unhelpfully. “Milk. Salt. Slightly too much salt. Ambrose is upset about something.”

Serenity laughs with her mouth full. She's still got her evening. She checks on it sometimes, the way you check a pocket for a key.

recalls.fallback: Serenity comes down to breakfast and sits on the end of the long table, swinging her boots, her map case beside her. Whatever November asked of her, she isn't saying. She eats her porridge all the way to the bottom of the bowl.
