storyScenes.title: Something Somebody Used to Make
storyScenes.opening:
It's All Souls. That's the night, in the old stories, when everybody who used to sit at your table comes back to see how you're getting on.

I don't know about that. I'm a book. But I know about this.

Somebody used to make something for you. It doesn't have to be anything special. It almost never is. Toast cut into soldiers. A soup when you were ill. The sandwich in your school bag. A cake on one particular day of the year that only ever smelled like that on that day.

Some of the people who made those things are far away now. Some of them are gone. Some of them are in the next room and haven't made it in years.

Make it. This week, if you can. It doesn't have to be right. It'll be nearly right, and nearly right is the whole point.

Then come back and give me one sentence about it. What it smelled like, maybe. That's the bit I can't get by myself.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Make something somebody used to make for you. Bring back one sentence about it.
storyScenes.braidText: You made something somebody used to make for you, and brought back what it smelled like.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: I've got it. Ambrose would say that's the whole of cooking: putting something back on the table that was missing.

storyScenes.title: Rescue a Recipe
storyScenes.opening:
There's a recipe near you that's in danger.

It isn't written down anywhere. Somebody makes it by feel. They've made it a hundred times. If you asked them how much salt, they'd say “enough,” and hold up a pinch of air.

Those are the ones that go first. They live in one person's hands, and hands get old, and move away, and stop.

Find one. Ask somebody how they make the thing they make. Your grandad's chilli. A friend's soup. The thing somebody at work brings to every party. Your own, even, if you're the only one who knows it.

Write down what they tell you, exactly as they say it. *Enough* is a real measurement. *Till it looks right* is a real time.

Then bring me one sentence: whose it is, and what it's called. I'll keep it where it can't go missing.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Ask somebody how they make the thing they make. Write it down. Bring back whose it is.
storyScenes.braidText: You rescued a recipe that only lived in somebody's hands, and brought back whose it was.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: Kept. Safe now. The Cookery's got one more page it didn't have before, and so have I.

storyScenes.title: Feed Somebody
storyScenes.opening:
Ambrose has a rule. He's never written it down, so I'm writing it down for him.

When somebody's having a hard time, don't ask them what's wrong. Put something in front of them. Then walk away before they can make a fuss.

That's all. That's the rule.

This week, feed somebody. Make something and give it away. A plate. A jar. A slice of something in a napkin. Toast counts. A cup of tea left by somebody's elbow counts.

Don't wait to be thanked. Ambrose never does.

Then give me one sentence about who you fed. You don't have to say their name if you don't want to. Just what you gave them, and what their face did.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Make something and give it to somebody. Bring back one sentence about what their face did.
storyScenes.braidText: You fed somebody and walked off before they could make a fuss.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: That's the whole trick. Ambrose would say so, if he ever said anything about it.

storyScenes.title: Set a Place
storyScenes.opening:
Ambrose sets a place at the long table for whoever's missing. He doesn't say who. Everybody knows.

You can do it too, if you want. One meal this week. Put out one more plate, or one more cup, or just a spoon. For somebody who used to sit with you, or somebody far away, or somebody you haven't met yet.

You don't have to tell anybody why. You don't have to tell me who.

If you want to, bring me one sentence afterwards. What you put out. Or nothing at all. Some places at the table are meant to stay quiet.
storyScenes.missionInvitation: Set one more place at one meal this week, for whoever's missing.
storyScenes.braidText: You set a place at the table for whoever's missing.
storyScenes.missionKeptResponse: I've kept it. I won't say who it was for. Nobody ever does.

storyScenes.title: The Cross off a Soul Cake
storyScenes.opening:
At the end of All Souls week there was one soul cake left.

Ambrose found it at the back of the bread crock, gone hard as a roof tile. He doesn't throw food away. He broke it in half over the hens' bucket, and a little piece of the top flew off and landed in my gutter, and stuck.

It's the bit with the cross on. Two cuts in brown crust, the shape a knife makes when somebody means it. The old Academy cut that cross so the cake would know who it was for.

I've kept it there. It's gone soft with my keeping. It still smells, very faintly, of nutmeg and the end of a long day.

storyScenes.title: Slip Number Seven
storyScenes.opening:
Serenity didn't open the rest of Soren's slips. She kept the first one in her pocket, and the other eight stayed on the dresser in their row, folded, beside their spoons.

The morning after, they were gone. All but one. Number seven had slid down behind the bread crock, and when Penny moved the crock to dust, it fell out and landed open, right on my leaf.

There wasn't a taste on the seventh spoon. Soren left it empty. The slip says, in his small careful hand:

*This one's warm. That's all. Hold it.*

She couldn't taste anything, then. But she could feel warm. He'd worked that out before anybody.

I haven't told her I've got it. I don't think it's mine to give.

storyScenes.title: A Very Clean Spoon
storyScenes.opening:
After Serenity went up to bed that night, the Guest washed her spoon.

It didn't have to. Ambrose washes everything in the morning. But it took the spoon from beside her empty bowl and scrubbed it, round and round, slowly, the way it scrubs the pots, for longer than any spoon has ever needed.

In the morning it was back in the drawer with the others. You can tell which one. It shines like a puddle with the sky in it. When I'm open on the dresser, I can see my own leaves in the back of it, upside down.

Nobody uses it. Everybody knows which spoon it is, and nobody ever says.

I've kept the shine of it.

storyScenes.title: The Napkin Hat
storyScenes.opening:
Ambrose left the empty place at the long table all night, the way he always does. The plate still full. The candle out. The napkin folded into its little hat.

In the morning, the napkin hat had moved.

Not far. It was in the very middle of the plate now, where it hadn't been. As if somebody had sat down in the night, and picked it up, and looked at it a while, and put it back. Exactly. Very gently.

Ambrose saw it. He didn't say anything. He cleared the plate and shook out the napkin and put it in the wash with all the others.

But I'd already got the creases. I've kept them, every fold, in case anybody wants to know how it was done.

bleedArticles.title: A Guest at the West Door
bleedArticles.body:
The Kitchens' west door was opened on All Souls' Eve for the first time in living memory. A visitor knocked three times and recited the souling rhyme. Ambrose Trencher gave the visitor a soul cake and a seat by the fire, and did not ask a name.

The visitor is small, wears a green coat with brass buttons, and has remained by the fire since. Students have taken to calling the visitor the Guest. The Bleed will do the same until better information is available.

Every pot in the Kitchens has been found scrubbed each morning since. Mr Trencher has declined to say who scrubbed them. On the evidence, he does not know.

Asked whether he would ask the Guest's name, Mr Trencher said, “When it's eaten.” The Guest has eaten a great deal.

bleedArticles.title: Letters Missing from The Middlemost Cookery
bleedArticles.body:
On Bonfire Night this correspondent found a letter missing from Ambrose Trencher's copy of *The Middlemost Cookery*. The T had gone from treacle on the page for parkin. The page was whole on Sunday. The Bleed checked.

The gap is clean. The paper is undamaged. There is no smudge, no tear, and no ink on anyone's fingers.

Professor Lydia Boggle has confirmed that, under the house rules, a visitor who has eaten at the hearth for three nights may not be turned out. The Guest has eaten at the hearth for considerably more than three.

Professor Momort has asked students not to thank the Guest for anything. Asked why, he said, “Old kitchen manners.” Asked what that meant, he left.

bleedArticles.title: The First Week, Attested
bleedArticles.body:
For those catching up: on All Souls' Eve a small visitor in a green coat came to the Kitchens' west door and was fed. Nobody knows its name. The Academy calls it the Guest.

Since then, the Kitchens' pots have been scrubbed each night by nobody. By the oldest house rule the Guest may not be turned out. On Bonfire Night a letter went missing from Ambrose Trencher's cookbook, *The Middlemost Cookery*. More have gone since.

The Bleed is keeping count. Readers are asked not to thank the Guest, on the advice of Professor Momort.

bleedArticles.title: Martinmas Supper Tastes of Nothing
bleedArticles.body:
Wednesday's Martinmas supper in the Great Hall tasted of nothing. This is not an opinion. The Bleed interviewed eleven diners at four tables. All eleven described the goose as the shape of goose.

Pippa Pilcrow attributed the fault to the gravy's punctuation. Serenity Brown told the Hall she has tasted nothing since October, and that everybody now knew what that was like.

Several diners report that the Guest went round the Hall filling water glasses before the food went flat. The Bleed records this. It draws no conclusion from it.

Mr Trencher halved the loaves for Martinmas, as is the custom, and left the second halves by the Kitchen door. By morning the basket was empty and the cloth was folded.

bleedArticles.title: Two Hundred and Fourteen
bleedArticles.body:
For those catching up: a visitor called the Guest came to the Kitchens on All Souls and cannot be turned out under the house rules. Since then the Academy's food has gone flat and letters have vanished from *The Middlemost Cookery*.

This correspondent counted them: two hundred and fourteen. The only recipes keeping their letters were the ones somebody was still cooking.

The Academy is now cooking a great deal. Wicker Eddies has made an omelette. Letters are coming back. The count is on the Kitchen door: missing, and restored.

bleedArticles.title: A Wish Said Aloud
bleedArticles.body:
The Academy stirred the Christmas pudding on Stir-up Sunday, east to west, as is the custom. Every resident took a turn. Most made a wish and kept it.

The Guest took a turn as well, and said its wish aloud. It said: home. The Bleed is aware that wishes said aloud are not supposed to come true. It reports the wish anyway, because it was said in front of fifty witnesses.

The Headmistress was seen in the Kitchens' doorway during the stirring. She did not come in. This is the first time she has been seen on the Kitchen stairs this month. The Bleed does not know why, and will not guess.

That night a page came clear in *The Middlemost Cookery*, under the endpaper, after thirty years.

bleedArticles.title: The Week of the Page
bleedArticles.body:
For those catching up: the Guest has lived in the Kitchens since All Souls. The Academy's food went flat and letters vanished from *The Middlemost Cookery*, until the whole Academy began cooking to bring them back.

On Stir-up Sunday the Guest said its wish aloud: home. That night a page under the cookbook's endpaper came clear for the first time in thirty years. It is titled *A Bowl for the One Who Keeps the Pots.*

Mr Trencher has read it a great many times. He has bought oats.

bleedArticles.title: The Bowl, and After
bleedArticles.body:
For those catching up: a visitor came to the Kitchens' west door on All Souls and stayed the month. The Academy called it the Guest. While it stayed, food went flat and *The Middlemost Cookery* lost its letters, until the Academy cooked them back.

On the last day of November Ambrose Trencher cooked the page he had waited thirty years to cook: oats in milk, with salt, honey, butter and cold cream round the edge. He set it on the hearth. He did not say who it was for.

By morning there was a white bowl on the west step, with a black thorn beside it. This correspondent has filed it under Unattributed.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: FOR EXCHANGE: A Bonfire Night toffee hammer, slightly sticky, for anything at all that isn't sticky. W. E.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE HAMMER NOTICE: Exchanged for a bag of toffee. W. E. is aware of the irony and would like it left alone.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: NOTICE: The west windows in the Kitchens are to stay shut. Spoons are holding them. Do not borrow the spoons. Prof. L. Boggle.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE WINDOWS NOTICE: The spoons have been returned. The windows are shut. There was frost on the inside anyway.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: LOST: The taste of goose. Last seen at the Martinmas supper. If found, please return to the Great Hall, any table.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE GOOSE NOTICE: Nothing found yet. The goose sends its regrets.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: FOUND: A brass button, green thread still in it, on the west step. The owner may apply to the Kitchens. The owner probably knows.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE BUTTON NOTICE: Nobody applied. The button's been sewn back on. Nobody saw who did it.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: WANTED: Somebody who knows how much a pinch is. P. Pilcrow, deeply concerned.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE PINCH NOTICE: Professor Boggle says it's what fits between finger and thumb. Pippa has asked whose finger. The matter is unresolved.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: WANTED: One onion that doesn't make anyone cry. Will trade a spoon that doesn't burn. W. Eddies.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE ONION NOTICE: No such onion exists. Professor Boggle recommends a cold onion, a sharp knife, and accepting the rest.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: WANTED: Recipes that aren't written down anywhere. Especially your nan's. Apply to the Kitchen door. A. Trencher.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE RECIPES NOTICE: Fourteen have come in. One is just the word ENOUGH, written very large. Ambrose says it's the best of the lot.

bleedArticles.title: Classified
bleedArticles.body: LOST: Nine teaspoons. No, wait. Found. Please leave them exactly where they are. Thank you. I mean: I'm grateful.
bleedArticles.reply: REPLY TO THE TEASPOONS NOTICE: The teaspoons remain on the dresser. Someone has added a tenth. Nobody's owned up.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: Read your front page over the porridge pan. {possessive} {weekday} sounds like it wanted feeding. Did anybody feed it? Somebody should've.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: That photograph. Was anybody eating? You can always tell a good day by whether there's a plate in it somewhere.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: “{word}”. I'd put that in a soup. I'd put most things in a soup, but I'd put that in first.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: I've filed {possessive} quotation under evidence. Was it written before supper or after? It matters more than people think. I'd like to know.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: {Sky} lowers the appetite by a measurable amount. I've measured it. Ambrose says I'm wrong. He's put the soup on anyway.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: “{word}” is a plain, useful sort of word. Those are the ones that do the work. I've pinned it up inside the Pantry door.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: A page made by hand, in a month like this one? Somebody in your house knows what hands are for. Tell them to scrub the pots too.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: Did anybody ask {subject} what they needed on {weekday}? I'm asking. You don't have to answer. It's just nice to be asked.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: I looked at the photograph for ages. Who isn't in it? There's always somebody who isn't in it. I hope they got fed.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: You did the dare. I made an omelette. We've both had a week. Mine had eggshell in it. Yours probably didn't. Show-off.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: I read your front page while burning toast. Both went fine. I mean the front page went fine. The toast's in the bin.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: I can't taste anything this month, so tell me what “{word}” tastes like. I'm serious. Write it in the margin.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: {Sky}? I went up on the roof in it with my tongue out. Still nothing. Still going up there.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: “{braid}”. I've made a slip for it. Number ten. There were only meant to be nine.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: Your quotation has exactly the right number of commas. I counted. I wanted to add one. I didn't. Growth.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.byline: Prof. T. Mook, the Registry (in red ink)
bleedArticles.body: Your correspondent hasn't filed. Neither, entirely, has The Middlemost Cookery. The Registry is having a difficult month.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.body: {spell} has been entered in the register. So has a soul cake, a parkin, and a stranger in a green coat. The register's getting heavy.

bleedArticles.title: Letter
bleedArticles.byline: Dr. S. Inkrest, the Still Room
bleedArticles.body: Nothing filed yet tonight. The Kitchen lamp's on anyway. Come down if you can't sleep. There's usually soup.

banter.caption: Thornwave. Trencher's baking soul cakes. Forty of them. I asked him who they're for. He said “whoever knocks.” Nobody knocks on the Kitchens. There's no door there anybody uses. Here's one with a bolt on it.

Fae-Fi, and a notice from the Kitchens. There's a new kitchen hand. Don't thank it. Don't leave it clothes. If you really have to say something, say you're grateful, and then go and do the washing up. That's it. That's the notice. Here's a song about bees.

Mothlight. It's very late. The Kitchens' light is on again. If you're down there at this hour, and something at the sink is kind enough to offer you anything at all, finish your soup first. Always finish your soup.
I stirred the pudding. I made a wish. Not telling you. Penny says it has to hang in a cloth till Christmas before it counts. So do the rest of us. Here's the track.
Fae-Fi. The bowl's back on the dresser, washed and dry. Nobody saw who washed it. Trencher says that's how it's meant to be, and he'd like his kitchen back now, please. Here's something warm.

wonderLines.line: The onion went clear in the butter, the way a shy person does once they've decided to stay.
The garlic had been sitting in its papery coat all week, waiting for somebody brave.
The butter went from quiet to a small busy hiss, like rain finding a tent.
The honey took its time leaving the spoon, the way you do from a warm room.
The oats had been in the jar since summer, dreaming of milk.
The spices in the jar remembered ships, and said so, the moment the lid came off.
Cut across the middle, the apple had a star inside it, and it'd been keeping quiet about it all along.
The jar of jam had been holding a whole August in the dark for somebody.
The pot hung on its hook, scrubbed and shining, and wouldn't say who'd done it.
The ladle had dipped into a thousand suppers and remembered every one as the best.
The flour got onto everything it could reach, the way news does.
The salt sat in its cellar like a gatekeeper, deciding who got in.
The gravy went on and on round the plate, because nobody had given it a full stop.
The pudding steamed in its cloth all night, keeping everybody's wishes warm.
The leftovers in the fridge were the best part of yesterday, waiting to be asked back.
The bowl on the hearth had been set down for somebody, and everybody knew who.
The old recipe knew the way back to a kitchen that wasn't there any more, and went anyway.
The napkin had been folded into a little hat for somebody who wasn't coming, and wore it proudly.

notePrompts.text: What did the kitchen smell like tonight?
Who did you feed today? Who fed you?
What does your house smell like on the one day a year it smells like that?
Something you made with your hands. What did they do?
Write down something somebody used to make for you.
A recipe that isn't written down anywhere. Write it down here.
How much is enough? Write the amount the way the person who taught you would say it.
Who would you set an empty chair for?
What do you eat when it's cold?
The sound of something cooking. Describe it without naming the food.
The best table you ever ate at. Who was there?
Something that went wrong in the kitchen, and what you did about it.
Say I'm grateful to somebody. Write down who, and for what.
A wish you'd make if you were stirring the pudding. You don't have to say it out loud.
Draw the bowl you'd leave out for whoever keeps your house.
